questions.stem: Which structural feature lets a red cell pass vessels narrower than itself?

options.A: About 40% excess surface area for its volume
options.B: About 40% excess volume for its surface area
options.C: A rigid membrane that resists shear
options.D: High cytoplasmic viscosity from a high MCHC

questions.explanation: The red cell has about 40% excess surface area (about 140 µm² for about 90 fL), low cytoplasmic viscosity (regulated MCHC) and a strong yet deformable membrane. B: The excess is in surface area. C: It must be deformable. D: Viscosity is kept low. E: Red cells have no mitochondria.

questions.stem: Why are old red cells removed from the circulation?

options.B: The nucleus reappears and stiffens the cell
options.C: ATP rises and the pump overworks
options.D: Complement lyses cells older than 120 days
options.E: Trimmed membrane makes them more spherical

questions.explanation: With age, macrophages trim small pieces of membrane, so old cells become more spherical and are removed. A: That is oxidant damage. B: Mature red cells have no nucleus. C: Not the mechanism given. D: Not the mechanism given.

questions.stem: Which statement about the red cell membrane is correct?

options.A: An actin network is tied to the bilayer by horizontal links such as hemoglobin
options.B: A spectrin network is tied to the bilayer by vertical links such as ankyrin and band 3
options.C: A spectrin network floats free of the bilayer
options.D: The bilayer is three-dimensional and rigid

questions.explanation: The lipid bilayer is anchored to the skeleton by vertical links (ankyrin and 4.1R complexes, band 3). The cytoskeleton is a 2-dimensional elastic network of spectrin; defects cause spherocytosis and elliptocytosis. A: Not as described. C: It is anchored by vertical links. D: The skeleton is a 2-dimensional elastic network. E: Ankyrin is a linking protein.

questions.stem: How does the red cell use glucose?

options.A: About 10% in glycolysis; about 90% in the pentose phosphate pathway
options.B: About 50% in glycolysis; about 50% in the Krebs cycle
options.C: About 90% in glycolysis; about 10% in the pentose phosphate pathway

questions.explanation: About 90% of glucose goes through anaerobic glycolysis (ATP, NADH, 2,3-BPG, lactate) and about 10% through the pentose phosphate pathway (G6PD, NADPH, reduced glutathione). A: Reversed. B: There are no mitochondria. D: There are no mitochondria. E: Not as described.

questions.stem: Which product of glycolysis is matched with its function in the red cell?
questions.explanation: ATP powers the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and keeps the cell flexible; NADH keeps heme iron as Fe²⁺ (no methemoglobin); 2,3-BPG helps hemoglobin release O₂; NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway gives reduced glutathione. A: That is NADH. B: That is ATP. C: That is NADPH and reduced glutathione. E: Lactate leaves the cell.

questions.stem: How do G6PD deficiency and pyruvate kinase deficiency differ in mechanism and site of hemolysis?

options.A: G6PD: rigid cells, extravascular; PK: Heinz bodies, mostly intravascular
options.B: G6PD: low ATP, extravascular; PK: oxidant stress, extravascular
options.C: Both: Heinz bodies and intravascular hemolysis
options.D: G6PD: spherocytes, extravascular; PK: schistocytes, intravascular
options.E: G6PD: Heinz bodies, mostly intravascular; PK: rigid cells, extravascular

questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency: oxidant stress, Heinz bodies, bite cells, mostly intravascular hemolysis. PK deficiency: too little ATP, rigid cells removed by the spleen (extravascular). A: Reversed. B: The mechanisms are swapped. C: PK deficiency gives rigid cells removed by the spleen. D: Not as described.

questions.stem: When does hemolysis become hemolytic anemia?

options.A: When the red cell lifespan falls below 120 days

questions.explanation: Hemolysis is a shortened red cell lifespan from premature destruction; hemolytic anemia occurs when destruction outpaces the marrow's ability to increase production. A: That defines hemolysis. B: That shows marrow response. C: That is a sign of hemolysis. E: That is a marker, not the definition.

questions.stem: A patient has reticulocytosis, mild jaundice and gallstones but a normal hemoglobin. Which term applies?
questions.explanation: Compensated hemolysis: the marrow can raise output several-fold, so hemolysis may cause no anemia, only reticulocytosis, jaundice or gallstones. B: Hemoglobin is normal. C: Reticulocytes would not be raised. D: Reticulocytes would be low. E: Not the picture.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes the breakdown of the heme ring?

options.A: Unconjugated bilirubin, biliverdin, conjugation in the gut, urobilinogen in the liver
options.B: Biliverdin, unconjugated bilirubin on albumin, conjugation in the liver, urobilinogen in the gut
options.C: Biliverdin, conjugated bilirubin on albumin, deconjugation in the liver, stercobilin in urine
options.E: Biliverdin, urobilin in the spleen, bilirubin in the gut

questions.explanation: In macrophages, globin goes to amino acids, iron to transferrin, and the heme ring to biliverdin then unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin carried on albumin. The liver conjugates it; gut bacteria make urobilinogen; stercobilin colours stool and urobilin urine. A: Biliverdin comes first and conjugation is hepatic. C: Albumin carries unconjugated bilirubin; stercobilin is in stool. D: Not the order. E: Not the order.

questions.stem: Which type of gallstone is a consequence of chronic hemolysis?
questions.explanation: In hemolysis every step speeds up: high indirect bilirubin (jaundice), more urobilinogen in stool and urine, and pigment gallstones. A: Not the type linked to hemolysis. B: Those are renal. D: Those are renal. E: Not the type linked to hemolysis.

questions.stem: Which classification of hemolytic anemia by cause is correct?

options.A: Intrinsic: immune, mechanical or infectious damage, usually acquired
options.B: Extrinsic: membrane, enzyme or hemoglobin defects, usually inherited
options.C: Intrinsic: destruction inside vessels; extrinsic: destruction in the spleen
options.E: Intrinsic: membrane, enzyme or hemoglobin defects, usually inherited

questions.explanation: Intrinsic (intracorpuscular): defective red cells (membrane, enzyme, hemoglobin), usually inherited. Extrinsic (extracorpuscular): healthy red cells destroyed by outside factors (immune, mechanical, infectious, toxic), usually acquired. A: That is extrinsic. B: That is intrinsic. C: That is classification by site. D: PNH is an acquired intrinsic disorder.

questions.stem: Which site of hemolysis is the most common?
questions.explanation: Extravascular hemolysis (macrophages of the spleen, liver and marrow) is the most common. A: Less common. B: That is ineffective erythropoiesis. D: Not a site of hemolysis. E: Not as stated.

questions.stem: What makes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria unusual among intrinsic hemolytic anemias?

options.A: It is an inherited extrinsic disorder
options.B: It is the sole enzyme defect
options.D: It is an acquired intrinsic disorder

questions.explanation: Acquired intrinsic: PNH, with complement-sensitive red cells. Other intrinsic causes are usually inherited. A: It is acquired and intrinsic. B: It involves complement-sensitive red cells. C: Not stated; it is a red cell defect. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: Which causes are classed as macroangiopathic hemolysis?

options.C: Warm and cold red cell autoantibodies

questions.explanation: Extrinsic: immune (autoimmune, alloimmune, drug-induced), microangiopathic (DIC, TTP, HUS), macroangiopathic (prosthetic heart valves, hypersplenism), other (infections, toxins, venoms, liver and renal disease, burns). A: These are microangiopathic. C: These are immune. D: These are infections. E: Listed under other causes.

questions.stem: Which findings point to intravascular and not extravascular hemolysis?
questions.explanation: Intravascular: often acute and severe, raised free plasma Hb, hemoglobinuria (red–brown), hemosiderinuria later, haptoglobin very low or absent, schistocytes. Extravascular: mild to moderate, often chronic, no free Hb, haptoglobin normal or low, spherocytes. B: These suggest extravascular hemolysis. C: Seen in both. D: Seen in both. E: Seen in both.

questions.stem: Which examples are matched with the site of hemolysis?

options.A: Warm AIHA and hereditary spherocytosis: intravascular
options.B: ABO transfusion reaction and TTP: extravascular
options.D: Warm AIHA and hereditary spherocytosis: extravascular

questions.explanation: Intravascular: ABO transfusion reaction, G6PD crisis, TTP, PNH, malaria. Extravascular: warm AIHA, hereditary spherocytosis. A: They are extravascular. B: They are intravascular. C: They are intravascular. E: Listed as intravascular.

questions.stem: Which laboratory findings are shared by intravascular and extravascular hemolysis?

options.C: Reticulocytosis, high indirect bilirubin and high LDH
options.D: Schistocytes, low platelets and high D-dimer
options.E: Low reticulocytes, high ferritin and low LDH

questions.explanation: Both show reticulocytosis, high indirect bilirubin, high LDH and urobilinogen in stool and urine. A: These mark intravascular hemolysis. B: These fit extravascular hemolysis. D: These suggest DIC. E: Not hemolysis.

questions.stem: What must be ruled out in any acute-onset anemia before attributing it to hemolysis?
questions.explanation: Rule out bleeding in any acute-onset anemia. Hemolysis presents with anemia symptoms plus jaundice, dark or red urine, fever, chills, abdominal and back pain, splenomegaly and gallstones. A: Not acute in onset. C: Not acute in onset. D: Not acute in onset. E: Not acute in onset.

questions.stem: A child with autoimmune hemolytic anemia also has immune thrombocytopenia. What is this combination called, and what should be looked for?
questions.explanation: Evans syndrome is autoimmune hemolytic anemia plus immune thrombocytopenia; screen for immune dysregulation. Other red flags: recurrent infections, family history, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, masses. A: The search is for immune dysregulation. B: HELLP occurs in pregnancy. C: That is a microangiopathy with kidney injury. D: That is a separate entity.

questions.stem: Which marker is the most sensitive for hemolysis?
questions.explanation: Haptoglobin binds free Hb and is the most sensitive marker (low in hemolysis). Also: high reticulocytes, indirect bilirubin and LDH; plasma or urine Hb in intravascular hemolysis; urine hemosiderin in chronic intravascular hemolysis. B: Released from red cells but not the most sensitive. C: From heme breakdown but not the most sensitive. D: Marks chronic intravascular hemolysis. E: Reflects large reticulocytes.

questions.stem: In a hemolytic patient the reticulocyte count is low. Which explanation does the lecture give?
questions.explanation: Reticulocytes reflect the marrow response; they may be low early or with marrow suppression (e.g. parvovirus B19). A: Reticulocytes would be high. B: Reticulocytes would be high. C: Not the explanation given. E: Not the explanation given.

questions.stem: Why may the MCV be slightly high in hemolytic anemia?

options.E: Schistocytes are counted as large cells

questions.explanation: Anemia is usually normocytic; MCV may be slightly high because reticulocytes are large. B: Not the reason given. C: Spherocytes are small. D: Not the reason given. E: They are fragments.

questions.stem: Which test is matched with the diagnosis it points to?
questions.explanation: DAT: immune hemolysis. Coagulation tests, fibrinogen, D-dimer: DIC. ADAMTS13 <10%: TTP. Hb electrophoresis: sickle cell disease, thalassemia. EMA binding, osmotic fragility, high MCHC: hereditary spherocytosis. Enzyme assays: G6PD, PK. Flow cytometry: PNH. A: PNH uses its own flow cytometry. B: It points to TTP when below 10%. C: It points to immune hemolysis. D: They point to DIC.

questions.stem: When should G6PD activity be measured in a patient with acute hemolysis?

options.B: Before any transfusion, within the hour

questions.explanation: G6PD and PK enzyme assays detect enzyme deficiencies; test G6PD after the acute episode. A: The assay is advised after the episode. B: Not the advice given. D: Not the advice given. E: Not the advice given.

questions.stem: What do the direct and indirect antiglobulin tests detect?

options.A: Direct: antibodies in the patient's serum; indirect: IgG or C3 on the patient's red cells
options.B: Direct: IgG or C3 on the patient's red cells; indirect: antibodies in the patient's serum
options.C: Direct: free hemoglobin in plasma; indirect: haptoglobin
options.D: Direct: donor antibodies; indirect: donor red cells
options.E: Direct: IgM cold agglutinins; indirect: IgG warm antibodies

questions.explanation: DAT detects IgG or C3 already on the patient's red cells (agglutination with anti-human globulin = positive). IAT detects anti-red cell antibodies in the patient's serum and is essential for antibody screening and crossmatch. A: Reversed. C: Not what they detect. D: Not what they detect. E: Not the distinction.

questions.stem: Which features define warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia?

options.A: IgG binding at 37 °C; extravascular hemolysis with spherocytes
options.B: IgM binding below 30 °C; DAT positive for C3
options.C: Biphasic IgG after viral infection; intravascular hemolysis
options.D: IgG binding at 37 °C; intravascular hemolysis with schistocytes

questions.explanation: Warm AIHA is the most common type: IgG binds at 37 °C; DAT IgG ± C3; extravascular, the spleen makes spherocytes. Primary, or secondary to lupus, immune deficiency, lymphoma, infection, transplant, checkpoint inhibitors. B: That is cold agglutinin disease. C: That is paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria. D: It is extravascular with spherocytes. E: Not as described.

questions.stem: An elderly man has bluish fingers and ears in cold weather with anemia. The DAT is positive for C3 only. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.explanation: Cold agglutinins: IgM binds below about 30 °C and fixes complement; DAT C3 only; mainly extravascular (liver); acrocyanosis on cold exposure. Primary CAD is a clonal B-cell disorder in older adults; secondary to Mycoplasma or EBV. A: DAT would show IgG. B: That occurs in children after viral infection. D: DAT is not the diagnostic test there. E: Not the picture.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old has sudden red urine and anemia a week after a viral illness. A biphasic IgG antibody is found. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.explanation: Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria: biphasic IgG (Donath–Landsteiner) after viral infection in children; acute intravascular hemolysis, usually self-limited. A: That involves IgM, typically in older adults. C: Not a biphasic antibody. D: That follows bloody diarrhea with kidney injury. E: That is AIHA with immune thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: What is first-line treatment of warm AIHA?
questions.explanation: Warm AIHA: corticosteroids first line; add rituximab early in severe disease; then immunosuppressants; splenectomy less often. A: Used less often, later. B: That is for TTP. C: That is for cold agglutinin disease. E: That is a C5 inhibitor for PNH and atypical HUS.

questions.stem: How is cold agglutinin disease managed?

options.A: Corticosteroids first line; splenectomy if refractory

questions.explanation: Cold agglutinin disease: avoid cold; warm IV fluids and blood; rituximab-based therapy targets the B-cell clone. A: That is the warm AIHA approach. B: That is for TTP. C: That prevents Rh(D) sensitization. D: Not sufficient.

questions.stem: Which new drug is matched with its target and disease?

options.A: Nipocalimab: C1s, cold agglutinin disease; sutimlimab: FcRn, warm AIHA
options.B: Nipocalimab: C5, PNH; sutimlimab: factor B, PNH
options.C: Sutimlimab: vWF, TTP; nipocalimab: ADAMTS13, TTP
options.D: Nipocalimab: FcRn, warm AIHA; sutimlimab: C1s, cold agglutinin disease
options.E: Nipocalimab: CD20, warm AIHA; sutimlimab: CD20, cold agglutinin disease

questions.explanation: Nipocalimab (FDA Aug 2026): first approved drug for warm AIHA; blocks FcRn, lowering IgG autoantibodies. Sutimlimab (FDA Feb 2022): first for cold agglutinin disease; blocks C1s of the classical pathway. A: Reversed. B: Not their targets. C: Not their targets. E: CD20 is the rituximab target.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes into a red cell transfusion a woman develops fever, chills, dyspnea, red urine and a blood pressure of 55/40 mm Hg. What is the usual cause of this reaction?

options.E: ABO mismatch from a clerical error

questions.explanation: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (within 24 h): usually ABO-incompatible blood from a clerical or identification error; recipient IgM anti-A/B fix complement, causing intravascular hemolysis with fever, chills, flank pain, dyspnea, hypotension, red urine, DIC and renal failure. A: That causes a delayed reaction at 3–14 days. B: Not the cause given. C: Not an acute reaction. D: That causes HDFN.

questions.stem: What is the first action in a suspected acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?

options.A: Slow the transfusion and give antihistamine
options.B: Stop the transfusion and keep the IV line
options.C: Remove the IV line and send it for culture
options.D: Give a second unit of the same group

questions.explanation: Stop the transfusion; keep the IV line; recheck patient and unit identity; give fluids for urine output; tell the blood bank. A: The transfusion must be stopped. C: The line is kept. D: Identity must be rechecked. E: Not the first action.

questions.stem: A chronically transfused patient develops jaundice, a falling hemoglobin and a newly positive DAT 8 days after transfusion. Which mechanism fits?

options.A: Anamnestic rise of an alloantibody such as Kidd

questions.explanation: Delayed reaction (3–14 days): anamnestic rise of an alloantibody (e.g. Kidd, Rh) from earlier transfusion or pregnancy; extravascular; falling Hb, jaundice, new positive DAT. Prevent with extended antigen matching. B: That causes an acute reaction. C: Not the mechanism. D: That is PNH. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: What is hyperhemolysis in sickle cell disease, and how is it handled?

options.A: Donor red cells are destroyed, patient cells spared; transfuse more
options.B: Patient red cells sickle in the spleen; exchange transfusion
options.C: Donor and patient red cells are destroyed; avoid further transfusion
options.D: Donor platelets are destroyed; give platelets
options.E: Complement lyses donor cells; give eculizumab first line

questions.explanation: Hyperhemolysis in sickle cell disease: donor and patient cells are destroyed; avoid further transfusion if possible. A: Patient cells are destroyed too, and transfusion is avoided. B: That is sequestration. D: Not hyperhemolysis. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: In hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, which antigen system is the most severe and which the most common?

options.A: Rh(D) is the most severe; ABO is the most common
options.B: ABO is the most severe; Rh(D) is the most common
options.C: Kidd is the most severe; Rh(D) is the most common
options.D: Rh(D) is both the most severe and the most common
options.E: ABO is both the most severe and the most common

questions.explanation: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta against fetal red cell antigens inherited from the father. Rh(D) is the most severe; ABO is the most common (usually mild). Risks: hydrops, kernicterus. Prevention: anti-D immunoglobulin for Rh(D)-negative mothers. B: Reversed. C: Not as stated. D: ABO is the most common. E: Rh(D) is the most severe.

questions.stem: How does a positive DAT change the management of neonatal jaundice (AAP 2022)?

options.A: It is reassuring, so phototherapy thresholds are higher
options.C: A neurotoxicity risk: lower phototherapy thresholds
options.E: It has no effect on thresholds

questions.explanation: Isoimmune hemolysis (positive DAT) is a neurotoxicity risk factor: lower phototherapy thresholds, and escalate care as bilirubin nears the exchange level. A: It lowers the thresholds. B: Care is escalated as bilirubin nears the exchange level. D: Phototherapy is used earlier. E: It lowers them.

questions.stem: Which drug is matched with its mechanism of immune hemolysis?

options.B: High-dose penicillin: autoantibody; fludarabine: drug adsorption
options.C: Methyldopa: drug adsorption; penicillin: immune complex
options.E: Piperacillin: autoantibody; checkpoint inhibitors: drug adsorption

questions.explanation: Drug-dependent antibodies (immune complex, often intravascular and severe): ceftriaxone (notably in children), piperacillin, cefotetan. Drug adsorption (extravascular): high-dose penicillin. Drug-induced autoantibody (like warm AIHA): methyldopa, fludarabine, checkpoint inhibitors. Stop the drug. A: Reversed. B: Reversed. C: Not as listed. E: Not as listed.

questions.stem: What does the combination of schistocytes and thrombocytopenia mean?
questions.explanation: Schistocytes + thrombocytopenia = thrombotic microangiopathy until proven otherwise (DIC, TTP, HUS; also malignant hypertension, HELLP, drugs, transplant-associated TMA). A: That gives spherocytes and a positive DAT. B: That gives spherocytes. C: Not the meaning. D: Not the meaning.

questions.stem: Which laboratory pattern separates DIC from TTP and HUS?
questions.explanation: DIC: PT/aPTT prolonged, fibrinogen low. TTP: coagulation normal, ADAMTS13 <10%, brain and heart involvement, fever. HUS: coagulation normal, acute kidney injury. A: That defines TTP. C: That is the hallmark of HUS. D: Seen in each of them. E: Seen in each of them.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman has high fever, hypotension, coma, diffuse ecchymoses and low hemoglobin, white cells and platelets. The smear shows schistocytes. Which results and treatment are expected?

options.A: Normal fibrinogen and ADAMTS13 below 10%; plasma exchange
options.D: Normal PT and high haptoglobin; observation
options.E: Low fibrinogen, high D-dimer; treat the sepsis

questions.explanation: Severe infection with DIC: systemic activation of coagulation and fibrinolysis. Diagnosis: low platelets, prolonged PT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, schistocytes (ISTH score). Treat the cause; support with platelets, plasma or cryoprecipitate for bleeding. A: That is TTP. B: That is warm AIHA. C: That is STEC-HUS. D: Not DIC.

questions.stem: What is the normal function of ADAMTS13, and what happens when its activity is below 10%?

options.A: It cleaves ultra-large vWF multimers; microthrombi form
options.B: It cleaves fibrinogen; fibrin-rich thrombi block large veins
options.C: It activates complement; red cells lyse in the kidney
options.D: It cleaves ultra-large vWF multimers; bleeding from lack of vWF
options.E: It inhibits platelets; platelet count rises

questions.explanation: ADAMTS13 normally cleaves ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers; without it (<10% activity), platelet-rich microthrombi block small vessels, causing intravascular hemolysis, thrombocytopenia and ischemia of brain, heart and kidneys. Untreated mortality is about 90%. B: Its substrate is von Willebrand factor. C: Not its function. D: Lack of the enzyme causes thrombosis. E: Platelets are consumed.

questions.stem: Which statement about treatment of immune TTP is correct?

options.A: Wait for the ADAMTS13 result before plasma exchange
options.B: Give platelets and cryoprecipitate as first line
options.C: Give recombinant ADAMTS13 as standard for immune TTP
options.D: Start plasma exchange on clinical suspicion
options.E: Give caplacizumab without plasma exchange as the standard

questions.explanation: Immune TTP: therapeutic plasma exchange (removes antibody, replaces ADAMTS13), corticosteroids plus rituximab, caplacizumab (anti-vWF nanobody). Start on clinical suspicion (e.g. PLASMIC score). A registry suggests caplacizumab with immunosuppression may work without exchange, but plasma exchange remains standard. A: Treatment starts on clinical suspicion. B: That is support for DIC bleeding. C: It is for congenital TTP. E: Plasma exchange remains standard.

questions.stem: For which condition was recombinant ADAMTS13 approved in 2023?
questions.explanation: Recombinant ADAMTS13 (Adzynma, FDA Nov 2023): first enzyme replacement for congenital TTP, in adults and children. A: Standard treatment there is plasma exchange with immunosuppression. B: That is treated with C5 inhibitors. D: Not its indication. E: That is sutimlimab.

questions.stem: Which triad defines hemolytic uremic syndrome?

options.A: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and fever with coma
options.B: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury
options.C: Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets
options.D: Immune hemolysis, immune thrombocytopenia and neutropenia
options.E: Anemia, prolonged PT and low fibrinogen

questions.explanation: HUS triad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury. A: That suggests TTP. C: That is HELLP. D: That is not HUS. E: That suggests DIC.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old develops pallor and oliguria one week after bloody diarrhea. Which management point does the lecture stress?

options.D: Antimotility drugs to shorten the diarrhea

questions.explanation: STEC-HUS (about 90%): mostly young children, 5–10 days after bloody diarrhea; Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (e.g. O157:H7) or Shigella dysenteriae; supportive care with fluids and dialysis if needed; avoid antimotility drugs. B: That is for immune TTP. C: That is for atypical HUS. D: These are to be avoided. E: Not the treatment given.

questions.stem: What underlies atypical HUS, and what must be done before treating it with a C5 inhibitor?

options.A: Shiga toxin from E. coli; give antibiotics
options.D: Uncontrolled classical pathway; give C1 inhibitor
options.E: Uncontrolled alternative complement pathway; give anti-D

questions.explanation: Atypical HUS: uncontrolled alternative complement pathway (gene variants or anti-factor H antibodies); relapsing, with risk of kidney failure. Treatment: C5 inhibitors eculizumab or ravulizumab. Vaccinate against meningococcus before complement blockade. A: That is STEC-HUS. C: That is TTP. D: The alternative pathway is involved. E: Vaccination against meningococcus is needed.

questions.stem: Which cause of extrinsic hemolysis is matched with its category?

options.A: March hemoglobinuria: infection; spur cells: burns
options.D: March hemoglobinuria: mechanical; spur cells: liver

questions.explanation: Mechanical: prosthetic valves, march hemoglobinuria, ECMO. Infections: malaria, Clostridium perfringens, babesiosis. Toxins and venoms: snake and spider venom, copper, arsenic. Burns. Liver disease: spur cells (acanthocytes). Hypersplenism. A: Not as listed. B: Reversed. C: Reversed. E: Reversed.

questions.stem: A child with hereditary spherocytosis becomes suddenly more anemic with a very low reticulocyte count after a viral illness. Which complication is this?
questions.explanation: After a viral illness: paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, or parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis in chronic hemolysis. Newborns: HDFN, G6PD deficiency and hereditary spherocytosis can cause severe jaundice. A: That gives acute intravascular hemolysis in a previously well child. B: That follows transfusion in sickle cell disease. C: That adds immune thrombocytopenia. D: Not the complication named.

questions.stem: Which supplement is given in chronic hemolysis, and what precedes splenectomy?
questions.explanation: Treat or remove the cause; give folic acid in chronic hemolysis; immunosuppression for immune hemolysis; transfuse with caution in AIHA; chelation for iron overload; splenectomy for selected cases (vaccinate first); cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallstones. A: Iron is not the supplement named. B: Chelation is for transfusional overload. D: Not as stated. E: Not as stated.

questions.stem: What red cell transfusion threshold does AABB 2023 give for most hospitalized, stable adults?

options.A: A liberal threshold of Hb below 10 g/dL
options.B: A restrictive threshold of Hb below 5 g/dL
options.C: Hb below 8 g/dL for each patient
options.E: A restrictive threshold of Hb below 7 g/dL

questions.explanation: AABB 2023: restrictive threshold Hb <7 g/dL for most hospitalized, stable adults; 8 g/dL with cardiovascular disease or orthopedic surgery; always weigh symptoms. A: The threshold is restrictive. B: Not the value given. C: 8 g/dL applies with cardiovascular disease or orthopedic surgery. D: Not the guidance given.

questions.stem: Which targeted therapy is matched with its target in PNH?
questions.explanation: PNH: iptacopan (factor B, oral), danicopan (factor D, oral add-on), crovalimab (C5, subcutaneous); earlier standards eculizumab and ravulizumab (C5). Mitapivat: pyruvate kinase activator for PK deficiency and thalassemia. A: That is danicopan. C: That is crovalimab, eculizumab or ravulizumab. D: That is iptacopan. E: Mitapivat is a pyruvate kinase activator.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman has pallor, dark urine and icteric sclerae with a high indirect bilirubin. Besides hemolysis, which causes of high indirect bilirubin does the lecture list?

options.B: Biliary obstruction and acute viral hepatitis

questions.explanation: High indirect bilirubin: hemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis, Gilbert or Crigler–Najjar. Her most likely diagnosis is hemolytic anemia; next tests: reticulocytes, LDH, haptoglobin, smear, DAT. B: These raise direct bilirubin. C: These raise direct bilirubin. D: Not listed. E: That raises direct bilirubin.

questions.stem: Besides DIC, TTP and HUS, which conditions are listed as causes of microangiopathic hemolysis?

options.B: Warm AIHA and cold agglutinin disease

questions.explanation: Other microangiopathic causes: malignant hypertension, HELLP, drugs (e.g. calcineurin inhibitors), transplant-associated TMA. A: These are macroangiopathic causes. B: These are immune causes. D: These are enzyme defects. E: These are membrane defects.
